name: Insider Trading and Market Abuse Detection
title: Insider Trading and Market Abuse Detection
answer: Insider trading and market abuse detection covers the use of artificial intelligence to find suspicious trading patterns, communications and relationships that may indicate misuse of material non public information or other market misconduct. It spans surveillance of equities, derivatives, fixed income and crypto venues, and it reaches into chat, email and voice records where tips and coordination often surface. The work sits inside corporate governance and regulatory compliance, where exchanges, brokers, asset managers and regulators all run some form of monitoring. Detection is not proof of wrongdoing, it is a triage function that decides what a human investigator should look at next.

sections.body: Insider trading and market abuse detection covers the use of artificial intelligence to find suspicious trading patterns, communications and relationships that may indicate misuse of material non public information or other market misconduct. It spans surveillance of equities, derivatives, fixed income and crypto venues, and it reaches into chat, email and voice records where tips and coordination often surface. The work sits inside corporate governance and regulatory compliance, where exchanges, brokers, asset managers and regulators all run some form of monitoring. Detection is not proof of wrongdoing, it is a triage function that decides what a human investigator should look at next.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on trade and quote feeds, order book data, reference data and communications archives, usually pulled from surveillance platforms and market data vendors rather than built from scratch. Entity resolution links accounts, traders, counterparties and related parties so that a pattern can be traced across desks and legal entities. Compute is modest by machine learning standards, the harder problem is data quality, timestamp alignment and keeping the communications corpus searchable. Outputs land in case management tools where alerts are queued, assigned and closed with an audit trail.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Classic approaches start with rules and thresholds, such as trades placed shortly before announcements or activity clustered around a news event, and these remain the backbone of most surveillance. Machine learning adds anomaly detection on trading behaviour, graph analysis of who traded with whom and when, and natural language processing over communications to flag language that resembles tipping or coordination. Supervised models need labelled cases, which are scarce, so unsupervised and semi supervised methods are common, with investigators confirming or rejecting alerts to create feedback. The practical aim is to reduce false positives and surface the small number of alerts worth a human review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Surveillance generates personal data and legally sensitive records, so retention limits, access controls and data protection obligations apply alongside market conduct rules. Firms must be able to explain why an alert fired, which means model documentation, versioning and reproducible inputs matter as much as accuracy. Communications monitoring raises privacy and works council issues in several jurisdictions, and employee notice requirements vary. Regulators expect records to be preserved and produced on request, and enforcement actions increasingly turn on whether a firm's monitoring was adequate rather than on the model itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration between trade surveillance and communications monitoring, so a single alert can show the trade, the message and the relationship in one view. Regulators are also looking at how firms validate and govern the models they use for detection, which pushes documentation and testing closer to the centre of the work. Crypto and cross venue activity remain difficult because data standards are uneven and identities are harder to resolve. Generative tools may help investigators summarise cases and draft narratives, but the evidentiary standard stays with human review and the audit trail behind it.
